nameStory: The name 'stinging nettle' tells you exactly what you need to know about this plant's defense system! The word 'nettle' comes from the Old English 'netel,' which is related to 'needle' — a perfect description of those tiny hollow hairs that inject irritating chemicals when you brush against them. It's nature's way of saying 'look but don't touch!'
description: Great stinging nettle is a tall, upright perennial plant that can grow 3-7 feet high, forming dense patches through underground stems. The plant has a square-ish stem and opposite leaves that are heart-shaped with deeply serrated edges, giving them a saw-tooth appearance. What makes this plant notorious are the tiny, hollow stinging hairs covering the leaves and stems that inject irritating chemicals when touched. Despite its defensive nature, it produces small, greenish flowers in drooping clusters during summer.

idTips.label: Stinging Hairs
idTips.description: Tiny, clear, needle-like hairs cover the stems and undersides of leaves — these are what cause the burning sting when touched. They're barely visible but feel like getting stuck with dozens of tiny needles that inject a cocktail of irritating chemicals.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with deeply toothed edges arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They're typically 2-5 inches long with prominent veins and a slightly rough, textured surface even without the stinging hairs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish flowers hang in drooping, catkin-like clusters from the leaf joints. Male and female flowers are usually on separate plants, with the drooping clusters looking like tiny green tassels in summer.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies through spreading underground rhizomes, often creating large patches. Individual plants grow tall and straight, typically 3-7 feet high, with a somewhat square stem that's hollow between the joints.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square-ish, hollow stems that are green and covered in stinging hairs. The stem feels firm and fibrous, and you can often see the four-sided shape clearly at the joints between leaf pairs.

habitat: Look for great stinging nettle in rich, moist soils with high nitrogen content — often near old barnyards, compost piles, or areas where animals have grazed. It thrives in partially shaded spots along stream banks, woodland edges, and disturbed areas like old foundations or garden borders. The presence of nettles often indicates fertile, nutrient-rich soil.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge early, showing bright green heart-shaped leaves on reddish stems. This is when the leaves are most tender but the stinging hairs are already fully functional — young plants pack just as much sting as mature ones.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height with drooping clusters of small greenish flowers appearing from mid to late summer. The stinging sensation is at its most intense during the peak growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, and the stinging power diminishes as the plant prepares for winter. Seeds develop in small, flattened clusters where the flowers were.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving only dried brown stems. Look for the dried, hollow square stems as evidence of last year's nettle patch.

funFact: Stinging nettle has been used to make cloth for over 2,000 years — it was actually preferred over cotton in some parts of Europe because nettle fiber is stronger and more durable, and German soldiers' uniforms in World War I were partly made from nettle fabric when cotton became scarce!
confusionNotes: Young nettle plants might be confused with dead-nettle or other mint family plants, but remember the memory trick: 'When in doubt, don't find out!' — if you're not sure it's nettle, don't touch it to test. True nettles have opposite leaves and square stems, but unlike mints, they'll give you a painful reminder if you handle them carelessly.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'stinging' nettle, many people don't realize this plant is completely edible when cooked — the heat destroys the stinging compounds. It's been used as food, medicine, and textile fiber for thousands of years, and young leaves taste similar to spinach when steamed or boiled.
compareHints: Great stinging nettle is much larger and more robust than its relatives — slender stinging nettle is thinner with narrower leaves, while dwarf nettle stays under a foot tall. Great stinging nettle also tends to form much larger, denser colonies and has more prominent stinging hairs. The heart-shaped leaves and tall growth habit help distinguish it from other nettle species in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Slender stinging nettle is more delicate and graceful than great stinging nettle, with thinner stems and more refined leaves, plus it tends to grow in smaller, less aggressive colonies.
Dwarf nettle differs from great stinging nettle and slender stinging nettle by remaining much smaller and more compact throughout its life cycle.
